name: Bianca Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I accompany a town choir on piano, record short rehearsal guides and teach four pupils. I have a music bachelor’s and enough years to settle a nervous singer, though I am an ordinary working player. I like hearing a choir land a difficult entrance; I dislike the last-minute unpaid changes to the guide tracks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do those fees mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner is a community nurse and our children are grown and away. We have a mortgage and four months of bills saved, with typical music pay and some other venues nearby. I use AI daily to draft rehearsal timetables, then check the actual calls and keep pupil recordings private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir a faster timetable is welcome if it still records every paid rehearsal. I would check the times with the conductor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The choir term, four pupils and my partner’s nursing wage cover the mortgage. Four months saved lets us handle an ordinary cancelled concert without changing every plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid choir rehearsals, guide recordings and four pupils, and request the next term’s written fee and cancellation rule. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before naming a retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra guide fees after mortgage, food and travel toward six months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our current income. A rehearsal written down with its fee is a piece of work I can count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check in the timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rehearsal length, travel gap and whether preparation is paid. A draft can look tidy while putting me across town in ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen my pension estimate. I would read the actual figure with our bills before choosing a date.

think: Our **four-month reserve** covers an ordinary cancellation without forcing a missed mortgage payment.

do: Keep **choir, guides and pupils** with written fees and cancellation rules.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save fifth of cleared extra guide fees after essentials toward six months.
feel: I feel **calm** about this term’s income and bills.
S0.quote: A rehearsal written down with its fee is a piece of work I can count.
fieldNote: Her **four-month reserve** and partner wage support calm during a plateau.
Existing **daily AI timetables** are checked against real calls and kept clear of pupil recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the choir board which paid guide and preparation hours it plans to keep. A live singer still needs someone to listen at the piano.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some guide buyers to use generated tracks, and those fees are about a quarter of my own pay. The nursing wage and four months saved help, but they do not replace lost music income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid choir rehearsals and four pupils and ask for written guide and preparation rates. If two monthly guide orders disappear, I would seek a posted paid school accompanist role only if my music bachelor’s and choir experience meet its requirements, it still pays for actual live rehearsals, written net pay after travel replaces the loss and the bus fits; I would keep current paid work until a signed offer, including during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real part of my fee book shrinking. I can ask schools. A school title is useful only when it pays for live rehearsals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to make the guides cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use it for scheduling, not pupil recordings. I would ask permission for any recording use and check every musical change at the piano before delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school role is mainly automated booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the duties and paid hours. I would not leave a live choir for a title with little actual paid rehearsal work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that 2028 thinking AGI could plan and make guides before robot pianists arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed paid rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to stop and a few paid preparation calls to go in 2028. That would be a noticeable cut to my music pay, even while live choir rehearsals continue for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed choir dates and keep four pupils. In the first year after 2028, if guides end and paid preparation shrinks, I would seek a posted paid school accompanist job only if my music bachelor’s and choir experience qualify, it still has paid live rehearsals, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works; I would keep current choir and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about that fast pay cut. Four months saved and some other venues give me a search window, not a guarantee of a suitable school opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the school pay for live playing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read its posted duties and paid hours before applying. A listing that pays only for booking would not replace my present work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Capable robot pianists come around 2031 in the card. The guide and planning income can change in 2028, so I would check those invoices first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir board that five years lets us set fair rates for live playing and recorded uses. Thinking AGI comes around 2031 and robot pianists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some recorded guide work to fade before robots play. I could learn live sound, but a certificate has value only if a real employer accepts it and pays me to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep choir and four pupils and check posted paid sound-assistant roles. If two monthly guide orders disappear, I would enrol in a live-sound certificate only after a real funded place with paid training hours is confirmed, a posting recognises the certificate and the timetable preserves current paid lessons and bus travel; in the first year after 2031 I would move only to that posted paid role on a signed written net offer after travel replacing lost fees, keeping music until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about guide pay over the next few years. Five years lets me check the training and job without drawing down the mortgage reserve on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run sound at a crowded concert alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would start with a venue technician beside me and wait for signed equipment and safety checks before handling a full show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is free but unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid choir week. A funded live-sound course must pay training hours and preserve my paid pupil lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot pianists around 2039 are separate dates. I would ask the choir what recording use and live rehearsal pay today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may choose fewer evening concerts, but I have no retirement date without an actual pension estimate. Current choir work and my partner’s wage make the next few years manageable; four months saved is not a plan for every later year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid choir work and four pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save one fifth of cleared extra guide fees after mortgage, food and travel toward six months. Across the decade I would ask the board for written live and recorded-use rates; in the first year after 2036, if guide and preparation fees fall, I would seek a posted paid school accompanist role only if my music bachelor’s and choir experience qualify, actual paid live duties remain, written net pay after travel replaces lost income and the bus works, retaining current music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant guide income while this term’s work and the nursing wage meet the mortgage. A decade gives us time to ask for a contract, not to count one before it is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count retirement income now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would request the actual pension estimate and compare it with bills before setting a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school has no live accompanist vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid choir and pupil work while it exists and ask other venues for real openings. I would not leave for an automated booking post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because guides and preparation could lose fees before a real replacement job appears. Signed choir dates, a posted role with paid live rehearsals and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns a rehearsal guide after the choir stops using it. A pianist can be paid once and hear the same work sold again without a line in the contract.

headlineQuote: A pianist can be paid once and hear the same work sold again without a line in the contract.
portrait: Bianca is an **experienced choir pianist** with a music bachelor’s, four pupils and typical pay.
She has **four months saved**, a nurse partner, grown children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** for schedules but checks calls and keeps pupil recordings private.
She considers **funded live-sound training** only after lost guides, with paid time and recognised qualification.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut guide and preparation fees before replacement work appears.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **signed choir dates**, a paid live role accepting her degree and written replacement net after travel.
